A standard algorithm is a function in
that names an operation over a range instead of leaving you to write its loop again:

A lambda is an unnamed function object you write inline and pass to the algorithm; the compiler turns it into a class of its own, with one member per captured variable and a call operator built from its body. The problem this solves is a loop that hides what it does until you read every line of it, carries its own index to get wrong, and has no complexity guarantee beyond what you can prove yourself. Naming the operation instead,
for instance, tells the reader the intent before they read the lambda, and it can't forget a
The mechanism is the projection and the capture. Most range algorithms take a

needs no comparison lambda to write or get wrong. Where a lambda is still the argument, what it captures decides what it reads. A capture by value copies the variable into the lambda's own member when the lambda is created; a capture by reference stores a reference and reads the variable fresh on every call.

What it costs is two ways to get this wrong. A reference capture that is then stored, returned, or handed to another thread outlives the variable it reads, and dangles once that variable is gone. And a lambda carrying state, such as a counter, breaks what the range algorithms require of a predicate, that calling it twice with the same argument gives the same answer, so its results depend on how often the library copies it.
You meet both in the robot: a debounce lambda keeping state between calls must be passed by reference or with
